label: thm:BLparity
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:BLparity}
	For $n\in \mathbb{N}$, ${\rm ou}^*(n)$ is odd if and only if $6n-2$ is a square.
head: environment

label: thm:BL62
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: prob:BL
title: Problem
body_md:
\label{prob:BL}
	Determine exactly which of the congruences of \Cref{thm:BL62} {\rm (or \cite[Theorem 1.5]{BL})} can be strengthened to the corresponding progression with modulus $2p^2$.
head: environment

label: thm1
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: thm2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm2}
	Let $n\ge1$ be odd. We have,
	\[
	{\rm ou}^*(n)\equiv\begin{cases}1 \ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 2 \right)&\Leftrightarrow\ 3n-1\in S_1,\\
	2\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right)&\Leftrightarrow\ 3n-1\in S_2,\\
	0\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right)&\Leftrightarrow\ 3n-1\notin S_1\cup S_2.\end{cases}
	\]
head: environment

label: cor1
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor1}
Let $A,B\in \mathbb{N}_0$ with $A$ even and $B$ odd. Then, for $n\in \mathbb{N}_0$, we have
\[
{\rm ou}^*\left(An+B\right)\equiv 0\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right)\Leftrightarrow 3(An+B)-1\notin S_1\cup S_2.
\]
head: environment

label: C:GD2
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{C:GD2}
	Let $M\in\mathbb N$ with $\gcd(M,6)=1$, $\ell\ge5$ be a prime, and $j\in\mathbb{N}$ with $\ell\nmid j$. Assume that $\nu_\ell(M)$ is odd or that one of the following holds:
	\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\arabic*)}]
		\item $\ell\equiv1,11,17,19\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 24 \right)$;
		\item $\ell\equiv5,23\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 24 \right)$ and $\left(\frac j\ell\right)=-1$;
		\item $\ell\equiv7,13\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 24 \right)$ and $\left(\frac{3j}\ell\right)=-1$.
	\end{enumerate}
	Then, for all $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$, we have
	\[
	\mathrm{ou}^*\left(2M^2\ell^2n+R_{M,\ell,j}\right)\equiv0\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right).
	\]
Otherwise, for infinitely many $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$,
\[
\mathrm{ou}^*\left(2M^2\ell^2n+R_{M,\ell,j}\right)\equiv2\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right).
\]
head: environment

label: C:GD1
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{C:GD1}
	Let $\ell\ge5$ be prime and $j\in\mathbb N$ with $\ell\nmid j$, and assume that one of the conditions
	\textnormal{(1)--(3)} of \Cref{C:GD2} holds. Then, for $n\in\mathbb N_0$, we have
	\[
	\mathrm{ou}^*\left(2\ell^2n+R_{1,\ell,j}\right)\equiv0\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right).
	\]
	Otherwise, for infinitely many $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$,
	\[
	\mathrm{ou}^*\left(2\ell^2n+R_{1,\ell,j}\right)\equiv2\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right).
	\]
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: \Cref{C:GD1} settles \Cref{prob:BL}.
head: environment

label: lem1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem1}
We have,
\[
{\rm OU}(q)=\sum_{n\ge 0}(-1)^{n+1}q^{3n^2+2n}\left(1+q^{2n+1}\right)+\frac{1}{\left(q;q^2\right)^2_{\infty}}\sum_{n\ge 0}(-1)^n q^{n(n+1)}.
\]
head: environment

label: lem2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem2}
We have,
\[
\sum_{n\ge 0}q^{(2n+1)^2}=q\frac{\left(q^{16};q^{16}\right)^2_{\infty}}{\left(q^8;q^8\right)_{\infty}},\qquad \sum_{n\in \mathbb{Z}}(-1)^n q^{n^2}=\frac{(q)^2_{\infty}}{\left(q^2;q^2\right)_{\infty}},\quad (q)_{\infty}=\sum_{n\in \mathbb{Z}}(-1)^n q^{\frac{n(3n-1)}{2}}.
\]
head: environment

label: lem4
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem4}
We have,
\[
\frac{\left(q^2;q^2\right)^2_{\infty}\left(q^6;q^6\right)^2_{\infty}}{(q)_{\infty}\left(q^3;q^3\right)_{\infty}}=\sum_{n\ge 0}D_3\left(2n+1\right)q^n.
\]
head: environment

label: thm:watson
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: lem:phi4a
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:phi4a}
	We have,
	\[
	\frac{\left(q^2;q^2\right)_\infty\left(q^4;q^4\right)_\infty^6}{(q)_\infty^2\left(q^8;q^8\right)_\infty^4}=\sum_{j=0}^3 q^jF_j\left(q^4\right),
	\]
	where
	\begin{align*}
	F_0(q)&:=\frac{\left(q^2;q^2\right)_\infty^{15}}{(q)_\infty^8\left(q^4;q^4\right)_\infty^6},\quad F_1(q):=2\frac{\left(q^2;q^2\right)_\infty^{9}}{(q)_\infty^6\left(q^4;q^4\right)_\infty^2},\quad
	F_2(q):=4\frac{\left(q^2;q^2\right)_\infty^{3}\left(q^4;q^4\right)_\infty^2}{(q)_\infty^4},\\
	F_3(q)&:=8\,\frac{\left(q^4;q^4\right)_\infty^{6}}{(q)_\infty^2\left(q^2;q^2\right)_\infty^3}.
	\end{align*}
head: environment

label: lem3
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem3}
For $n\in \mathbb{N}$, we have that modulo $4$,
\[
\left(-q;q^2\right)^2_n-\left(-q^2;q^4\right)_n
\]
is an odd polynomial.
head: environment

label: lem5
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem5}
We have, for $n\in \mathbb{N}$,
\[
r_2(n)=4\sum_{d\mid n}\chi_{-4}(d).
\]

label: thm:d
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{thm:d}
	Let $n\in \mathbb{N}$. We have
	\[
	c_{\psi}(n)\ \text{is odd}\Leftrightarrow 24n-1=p^{4k+1}m^2\ \text{with}\ k\in \mathbb{N}_0\ \text{and for some prime}\ p,\ p\nmid m,\ m\in \mathbb{Z}.
	\]

label: L:CC
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: thm:apsy
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{thm:apsy}
	For $n\in \mathbb{N}_0$, we have
	\[
	c_\omega\left(8n+r\right)\equiv 0\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right)\ \ \text{with}\ r\in \{4,6\}.
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

label: assistlem0
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{W1} and \Cref{lem:phi4a}, we have
\[
\sum_{n\ge 0}c_\omega\left(4n+1\right)q^n=\frac{\left(q^2;q^2\right)_\infty^{9}}{(q)_\infty^6\left(q^4;q^4\right)_\infty^2}\equiv \frac{\left(q^2;q^2\right)^3_{\infty}}{\left(q\right)^2_{\infty}}\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right).
\]
This concludes the proof of the first claim. 

Next, again using \eqref{W1} and \Cref{lem:phi4a}, we obtain
\[
\sum_{n\ge 0}c_\omega\left(4n+2\right)q^n=2\frac{\left(q^2;q^2\right)^3_\infty\left(q^4;q^4\right)^2_\infty}{(q)^4_\infty}\equiv 2\left(q^2;q^2\right)_\infty\left(q^8;q^8\right)_\infty\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right).
\]
Letting $n\mapsto 2n$, the second claim follows.

Next, using the fact $(q)_\infty^{8}\equiv(q^2;q^2)_\infty^{4}\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 8 \right)$ and the definition of $F_0$ (see \Cref{lem:phi4a}), we get, for $n\in \mathbb{N}_0$, 
\[
F_0(q)\equiv\frac{\left(q^2;q^2\right)_\infty^{11}}{\left(q^4;q^4\right)_\infty^6}\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 8 \right).
\]
Thus, by \eqref{W1} and \Cref{lem:phi4a}, it follows that, for $n\in \mathbb{N}_0$,
\begin{align}\label{eqn10}
c_f(n)+2c_\omega\left(8n\right)=\left[q^{2n}\right]\left(F_0(q)\right)\equiv \left[q^{n}\right]\left(\frac{(q)_\infty^3}{\left(q^2;q^2\right)_\infty^2}\right)\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 8 \right).
\end{align}
By \eqref{W2}, we have, for $n\in \mathbb{N}_0$,
\[
c_f(n)+4(-1)^nc_\psi(n)=\left[q^{n}\right]\left(\frac{(q)_\infty^3}{\left(q^2;q^2\right)_\infty^2}\right).
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eqn10} and then multiplying by $\frac 12$, we conclude the proof of the third claim.

Finally, from \eqref{W1}, \Cref{lem:phi4a}, we get, $n\in \mathbb{N}_0$,
\[
2c_{\omega}\left(4n+3\right)+2(-1)^nc_\omega(n+1)=\left[q^{n}\right]\left(F_3(q)\right)\equiv 0\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 8 \right).\qedhere 
\]
head: environment

label: assistlem2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{assistlem2}
	For $n\in\mathbb{N}$ odd, we have
	\[
	{\rm ou}^*(n)\equiv \pm c_\omega(n)\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right).
	\]
head: environment

label: eqn3
title: Proof
body_md:
By \Cref{lem3}, we have that modulo $4$, for $n\in \mathbb{N}$,
	\[
	q^{2n+1}\left(\left(-q;q^2\right)_n^2-\left(-q^2;q^4\right)_n\right)\in \mathbb{Z}\left[q^2\right].
	\]
	Thus, by \eqref{eq:gf}, the definition of $\nu$ (see above \Cref{thm:watson}), and \eqref{thm:fine}, it follows that, for $n$ odd,
	\begin{align*}
	{\rm ou}^*(n)\equiv \left[q^{n}\right]\left(q\nu\left(-q^2\right)\right)\equiv \left[q^{n}\right]\left(q^3\omega\left(q^4\right)+q\frac{\left(q^8;q^8\right)_\infty^3}{\left(q^4;q^4\right)_\infty^2}\right)\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right).
	\end{align*}
	If $n\equiv 1\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right)$, comparing coefficients of $q^{4m+1}$ (with $m\in \mathbb{N}_0$) on both sides, by the first identity of \Cref{assistlem0}, we get
	\begin{equation}\label{eqn3}
	{\rm ou^*}(n)\equiv c_1(m)\equiv c_\omega(4m+1)=c_{\omega}(n)\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right).
	\end{equation}
	
	Similarly, if $n\equiv 3\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right)$, comparing coefficients of $q^{4m-1}$ (with $m\in \mathbb{N}$) on both sides, by the fourth identity of \Cref{assistlem0}, we obtain
	\[
	{\rm ou}^*(n)\equiv (-1)^{m} c_{\omega}(n)\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right).
	\]
	Combining this with \eqref{eqn3}, we conclude the proof.\qedhere
head: environment

label: lem:h
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:h}
	For $n\in \mathbb{N}_0$, we have
	\[
	c_2(n)\ \text{is odd}\Leftrightarrow 24n+5\in S^{[1]}_2.
	\]
head: environment

label: eqn11
title: Proof
head: environment

label: assistlem1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{assistlem1}
	Let $n\in \mathbb{N}$. Then, we have,
	\[
	c_\omega(n)\equiv 
	2\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right)\Leftrightarrow\ 3n-1\in S_2.
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, we consider the case $n\equiv 0\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 8 \right)$. Then, with $n=8m$ ($m\in \mathbb{N}_0$), $3n-1=24m-1$ is odd and by \Cref{assistlem0},  
\[c_\omega(n)\equiv2c_{\psi}(m)\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right).\]
Thus, to prove the claim, it suffices to show that
\[
c_{\psi}(m)\ \text{is odd}\Leftrightarrow 24m-1\in S_2.
\] 
This follows from \Cref{thm:d}.

Now, we assume that $n\equiv1\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right)$. With $n=4m+1$ ($m\in\mathbb N_0$) we have $3n-1=2(6m+1)$, and by
\Cref{assistlem0}, it suffices to prove that
\[
c_1(m)\equiv 2\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right) \Leftrightarrow 6m+1\in S_2^{[1]}.
\]
This holds by \Cref{L:CC}.

Next, we consider $n\equiv 2\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 8 \right)$. Then, with $n=8m+2$ ($m\in \mathbb{N}_0$), $3n-1=24m+5$ is odd and by \Cref{assistlem0},  
\[c_\omega(n)\equiv2c_{2}(m)\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right).\]
Thus, to prove the claim, it suffices to show that
\[
c_{2}(m)\ \text{is odd}\Leftrightarrow 24m+5\in S_2.
\] 
This follows from \Cref{lem:h}.

The case $n\equiv 4,6\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 8 \right)$ is trivial because of \Cref{thm:apsy} and $3n-1\notin S_2$. Assuming on the contrary that $3n-1\in S_2$. This directly implies that $p\equiv r\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 8 \right)$ with $r\in \{3,1\}$, respectively. Thus, $(\frac{-2}{p})=1$ and this contradicts the definition of $S_2$. 

Finally, we consider the remaining case $n\equiv 3\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right)$. Write $n=4m-1$ with $m\in\mathbb N$. Note that, for the base case $n=3$, the claim holds trivially. Moreover, $m<n$ (as
$n-m=3m-1\ge2$), so by the induction hypothesis
\begin{equation}\label{E:IH}
c_\omega(m)\equiv 2\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right)\Leftrightarrow 3m-1\in S_2 .
\end{equation}
By the fourth congruence of \Cref{assistlem0}, 
\[
c_\omega(n)\equiv(-1)^mc_\omega(m)\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right).
\]
Thus, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{E:red1}
c_\omega(n)\equiv2\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right)\Leftrightarrow c_\omega(m)\equiv2\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right) .
\end{equation}
Moreover, $3n-1=12m-4=4(3m-1)$. For $k\in\mathbb N$, it is straightforward to see that
\begin{equation}\label{E:red2}
4k\in S_2\iff k\in S_2.
\end{equation}
Combining this, \eqref{E:red1}, and \eqref{E:IH}, we conclude
\[
c_\omega(n)\equiv2\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right)\Leftrightarrow c_\omega(m)\equiv2\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right)\Leftrightarrow 3m-1\in S_2\Leftrightarrow 4(3m-1)=3n-1\in S_2.
\] 
This concludes the proof.\qedhere

title: Proof
body_md:
The first case trivially follows from \Cref{thm:BLparity}.

Now, we note that $S_1\cap S_2=\emptyset$ because for $m\in S_1$, $\nu_p(m)$ is even, whereas for $m\in S_2$, $\nu_p(m)$ is odd. Thus, to conclude the proof, it remains to show that, for $n\in \mathbb{N}$ odd, 
\begin{equation*}
{\rm ou}^*(n)\equiv 2 \ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right) \Leftrightarrow 3n-1\in S_2.
\end{equation*}
By \Cref{assistlem2} and \Cref{assistlem1}, we get
\[
{\rm ou}^*(n)\equiv 2 \ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right)\Leftrightarrow  c_{\omega}(n)\equiv 2 \ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right)\Leftrightarrow 3n-1\in S_2.\qedhere 
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $n\in\mathbb N_0$, $N:=2M^2\ell^2n+R_{M,\ell,j}$, $B:=M\ell^{-\nu_\ell(M)}$ and $K:=3\ell n+3j+\ell$. Then
\[
3N-1=2\ell^{2\nu_\ell(M)+1}B^2K,\qquad \ell\nmid BK,\quad K\equiv3j\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, \ell \right),\quad K\equiv\ell\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 3 \right) .
\]
Now, we show that
\[
N\ \text{is odd},\quad 3N-1\notin S_1,\quad 3N-1\notin S_2.
\]
Since $\gcd(M,6)=1$ and $\ell\ge5$ is prime, $\gcd(M\ell,6)=1$. Thus $\frac{2M^2\ell^2+1}3$ is odd and so, $N$ is odd. 

Next, note that $3N-1\notin S_1$ because $\nu_\ell(3N-1)$ is odd. 

Now, suppose that $3N-1\in S_2$. Write $3N-1=\varepsilon p^{4a+1}m^2$ with $\varepsilon\in \{1,2\}$.  Since, by definition of $S_2$,
\[
\nu_p\left(3N-1\right)=4a+1,\quad \nu_q(3N-1)\ \text{is even}\ \text{for all primes}\ q\neq p.
\] 
Moreover, as $\nu_\ell(3N-1)=2\nu_\ell(M)+1$ is odd, we get $p=\ell$. Thus, $\nu_\ell(M)=2a$ which contradicts the assumption that $\nu_{\ell}(M)$ is odd. Since $p=\ell$ and by definition of $S_2$, $(\frac{-2}\ell)=-1$, we have $\ell\equiv5,7\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 8 \right)$. In particular, condition (1) of \Cref{C:GD2} fails to hold as well. Note that
\[
2\ell^{2\nu_\ell(M)+1}B^2K=\varepsilon p^{4a+1}m^2\Rightarrow \varepsilon m^2=2B^2K\ \ \text{with}\ \varepsilon\in \{1,2\}.
\]
Write $K=\frac{\varepsilon s^2}{2}$ with $s:=\frac{m}{B}$ and $3\nmid s, \ell\nmid s$ because $K$ is not divisible by $3$ and $\ell$. For $K=s^2$,
\[
\ell\equiv K=s^2\equiv1\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 3 \right)\ \ \text{and}\ \ \left(\frac{-2}\ell\right)=-1\Rightarrow \ell\equiv5,23\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 24 \right)
\]
and $3j\equiv K=s^2\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, \ell \right)$ implies that $(\frac{3j}\ell)=1$. Thus condition (3) of \Cref{C:GD2} are not satisfied. Similarly, for $K=2s^2$, $\ell\equiv K=2s^2\equiv2\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 3 \right)$ and $(\frac{-2}\ell)=-1$ imply that $\ell\equiv5,23\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 24 \right)$ and $6j\equiv2K=(2s)^2\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, \ell \right)$ imply that $(\frac{6j}\ell)=1$. It is clear that, for $\ell\equiv5\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 24 \right)$, 
$(\frac2\ell)=(\frac3\ell)=-1$, and for $\ell\equiv23\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 24 \right)$, $(\frac2\ell)=(\frac3\ell)=1$.
So $(\frac6\ell)=1$ and $(\frac j\ell)=1$. Hence condition (2) of \Cref{C:GD2} fails to hold. Thus, for $3N-1\in S_2$, all the conditions in \Cref{C:GD2} fail to satisfy and thus contradicts the assumption. Therefore, $3N-1\notin S_2$ and by \Cref{thm2}, we conclude the proof.


Finally, assume that $\nu_\ell(M)=2a$ is even and that the conditions (1)--(3) do not hold. If $\ell\equiv7,13\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 24 \right)$ and
$(\frac{3j}\ell)=1$, we choose $s\in\mathbb N$ with $s^2\equiv3j\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, \ell \right)$, $s\equiv1\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 3 \right)$. Moreover, we set
$n:=\frac{s^2-3j-\ell}{3\ell}$. Then $K=s^2$ and $3N-1=2\ell^{4a+1}(Bs)^2$. 

Similarly, if $\ell\equiv5,23\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 24 \right)$ and
$(\frac j\ell)=1$, then $(\frac{6j}\ell)=1$ as $\left(\frac6\ell\right)=1$, so we choose $s\in\mathbb N$ with
$2s^2\equiv3j\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, \ell \right)$, $s\equiv1\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 3 \right)$. Letting $n:=\frac{2s^2-3j-\ell}{3\ell}$, $K=2s^2$ and
$3N-1=\ell^{4a+1}(2Bs)^2$. In both cases $n\in\mathbb Z$, since the numerator is divisible by $\ell$ and by $3$ (as $3\nmid$), and $n\in \mathbb{N}_0$ for $s$ sufficiently large. Since $\ell\nmid Bs$ and $(\frac{-2}\ell)=-1$, we get $3N-1\in S_2$ and so, by \Cref{thm2}, $\mathrm{ou}^*(N)\equiv2\ \, \left( \mathrm{mod} \, 4 \right)$. Since $s$ can be chosen arbitrarily large, this holds for infinitely many $n\in\mathbb{N}_0$.\qedhere
